notes:
I could only finish part of this. My search tool hit its usage limit early, so I fully read just one commentary: David Guzik's on Enduring Word. Even that page only loaded up to the start of verse 15. These notes cover **vv. 1–15**, all from that page. Where Guzik quotes older writers (Lenski, Alford, Luther, Spurgeon, Boice), I say so.

I didn't read anything for vv. 16–29, and I found nothing on where Protestant traditions differ or on Catholic, Orthodox, scholarly or popular modern views. Following your rules, I've left those out rather than fill them in myself. Unless I say otherwise, every note below comes from https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-2/

---

**v. 1**
- In 1:8–9 John said Christians still sin and that confessed sin is always forgiven. Here he adds that believers should still care about sin. He has already rejected sinless perfection, but he also insists we don't *have* to sin: God doesn't make believers sin, and everything needed for victory is ours in Christ. The weakness lies in our flesh, which will be made perfect at the resurrection.
- "Advocate" means a defence lawyer on our side. Guzik cites Lenski: in Demosthenes the word meant friends who step in to urge the judge to rule for the accused.
- Unlike a human lawyer, Jesus doesn't argue that we're innocent. He admits our guilt and pleads his own atoning sacrifice. "The Righteous One" means he is qualified to be our advocate because he is sinless. We need him because Satan accuses us (Rev 12:10). Guzik says to tell Satan's condemning accusations apart from the Holy Spirit's loving conviction.

**v. 2**
- In the Greek idea, "propitiation" was a gift to win over the gods. In the Christian idea, God himself provides the sacrifice, in Christ, that turns away his own just anger. Guzik quotes Alford: Christ's voluntary death as a sin-offering reconciled God and us and turned God's wrath away.
- **"Whole world":** Guzik reads this as a sacrifice made for everyone. Not everyone is saved, because atonement is not the same as forgiveness. His example is the yearly Day of Atonement (Lev 16:34): it covered all Israel, yet not every Israelite was saved. Sin need not stand between God and anyone who receives what God has provided.
- Guzik cites Alford quoting Luther: you are part of "the whole world," so you can't tell yourself Christ died for Peter and Paul but not for you.
- Guzik's site is in your Pentecostal/charismatic group. I couldn't read the Reformed side of this debate (limited atonement); possible sources are listed at the end.

**v. 3**
- The proof that we know God is that we keep his commands. Simple, loving obedience grows naturally out of fellowship with him.
- Grace doesn't make a converted person careless, because God changes the heart and writes his law on it. Guzik cites Spurgeon: people who say clearly preached grace leads to sin don't understand it, since few would hate God for being kind to them.

**v. 4**
- If someone's life isn't marked by obedience, it's fair to question his claim to know God.
- Guzik cites Spurgeon on the difference between knowing *about* Christ and knowing and trusting Christ himself. Only the second saves.

**v. 5**
- "Perfected" carries the idea of *mature*. A mature love for God shows itself in obedience, and that obedience and love give assurance that we are in him.
- Sin isn't removed until glory, but conversion changes how a believer relates to it. Guzik lists the changes: a Christian no longer loves sin, boasts about it, plans it, fondly remembers it, fully enjoys it, or rests easy in habitual sin. He quotes Spurgeon's line that sin is "dejected" in the Christian's heart but not "ejected."

**v. 6**
- Walking as Jesus walked doesn't mean copying his miracles. It means following his everyday walk with the Father, the steady, disciplined fellowship and obedience his power came from.
- Guzik cites Boice: this isn't sinlessness. It is moving in the direction of God's righteousness and growing more troubled by sin. Someone not doing so is not God's child.

**vv. 7–8**
- The command to love is *old* because the readers had heard it since they first became Christians. It is *new* because Jesus called it a new commandment (John 13:34). What was new was that Jesus showed a love never seen before, which we are to copy.
- Guzik uses the picture of the cross pointing four ways: a love wide enough for everyone, long enough for eternity, deep enough for the worst sinner, and high enough to bring us to heaven.
- "Darkness is fading": Guzik connects this to the darkness that marked humanity, especially the Gentiles, before the true light revealed Christ's finished work.

**v. 9**
- John has tested the readers by how they live. Later he will test them by doctrine. Here he tests them by their love for fellow Christians.
- Guzik cites Alford: "brother" here means fellow Christians, not "neighbour" in general, because John is writing about fellowship among believers.
- God is merciful to measure us by how we love other Christians. Yet it is also a hard test, because we often expect more of Christians.

**v. 10**
- Loving your brother shows you live in the light and aren't stumbling. Guzik compares the three tests (how we live, what we believe, and love) to the legs of a three-legged stool: all must stand together.

**v. 11**
- Without love, all is lost, even with right actions and right beliefs. Ministry and "being right" must not be put above love. Hatred can also take the form of indifference.
- John learned this himself. Early on he was a "son of thunder" who wanted to call down fire on people who rejected Jesus (Luke 9:54).

**vv. 12–14 (little children, fathers, young men)**
- Guzik reads these as stages of spiritual maturity.
- **Little children (v. 12):** new believers delight in having their sins forgiven. Forgiveness doesn't come in degrees, so even the newest Christian is completely forgiven. "For His name's sake" means the reasons for forgiveness lie in God, not in us.
- **Fathers (vv. 13a, 14a):** believers of long standing, whose maturity rests on years of knowing Christ personally. The repetition stresses that there is nothing "beyond" knowing him (compare Phil 3:10).
- **Young men (vv. 13b, 14b):** the front line in the battle with the evil one. Guzik cites Alford that youth is the time for active service. He warns against staying in spiritual childhood on purpose. Their strength comes from God's word living in them.
- **Children (v. 13c):** they put down deep roots in God's fatherly care. Guzik cites Spurgeon's picture of small children who are proud that their father is the greatest man alive.
- **Word note:** v. 12 uses *teknia* (stressing a child's dependence on a parent) and v. 13 uses *paidia* (stressing immaturity and need for teaching).

**v. 15 (only partly loaded)**
- Worldliness is singled out as a sin that especially threatens fellowship with God.
- "The world" here doesn't mean the planet or humanity, which God loves (John 3:16). It means sinful human society united against God. Guzik's early example is Babel (Gen 11): an anti-God leader, organised rebellion, and distrust of God's promise.

---
